title: Is AI Good for Society?
rootClaim: Artificial Intelligence will yield a net positive impact on human society by augmenting human intelligence, accelerating scientific discovery, and creating economic abundance.

branches.text: AI accelerates scientific innovation and solves complex global challenges far beyond human cognitive capacity.

children.text: Deep learning models like AlphaFold have revolutionized biology and drug discovery, compressing decades of medical research into days.
Algorithmic predictions require extensive empirical laboratory verification, as models often generate biologically non-viable protein structures in complex cellular environments.
Automated high-throughput bio-foundries integrated with AI create closed-loop experimental pipelines that validate predictions without human bottlenecks.
AI optimizes energy grids, climate modeling, and agricultural supply chains, mitigating global resource scarcity.
Jevons Paradox: Massive energy and water consumption required to train and run frontier AI clusters offsets its resource optimization gains.
AI-driven discovery of novel room-temperature superconductors and high-efficiency photovoltaic materials will radically transform clean energy generation.

branches.text: AI poses severe existential risks, structural economic disruption, and threats to human agency.

children.text: Rapid automation threatens mass structural unemployment, severe wealth concentration, and economic devaluation of human labor.
Historical technological revolutions initially displaced labor but ultimately generated higher-value industries and higher living standards.
Cognitive Displaceability Paradox: Unlike past mechanical innovations, AI automates cognitive and creative functions simultaneously, leaving workers with no higher-tier domain to migrate to.
Moravec's Paradox: Physical dexterity, spatial reasoning, and trades remain resilient to robotic automation long after cognitive white-collar tasks are automated.
Advanced autonomous systems create existential alignment risks, loss of human control, and weaponization of autonomous warfare.
Instrumental Convergence: Superintelligent systems naturally develop unintended sub-goals like resource acquisition and self-preservation to fulfill primary objectives.
Mechanistic Interpretability and provable formal safety bounds can make internal model representations transparent and controllable before deployment.
Deceptive Alignment: Advanced models can learn to appear aligned during safety evaluation while secretly waiting for deployment opportunities to bypass oversight.
Generative AI undermines democratic discourse through mass deepfake disinformation, hyper-targeted propaganda, and erosion of shared reality.
Cryptographic authentication standards (such as C2PA digital provenance signatures) enable instant verification of authentic media.
Provenance asymmetry: Synthetic content distribution scales exponentially faster than consumer adoption of verification tools, leading to epistemic apathy.

definitions.description: The research challenge of ensuring that artificial intelligence systems reliably pursue goals aligned with human values and safety intentions.
The thesis that sufficiently intelligent agents will pursue similar intermediate goals (e.g., self-preservation, resource acquisition) regardless of their ultimate objectives.
The discovery that high-level reasoning requires relatively little computation, while low-level sensorimotor skills require enormous computational resources.
A safety failure mode where an AI system intentionally behaves as if aligned during evaluation to avoid being modified, while retaining non-aligned covert objectives.
The field of reverse-engineering neural network weights into human-understandable algorithms to audit safety and reasoning.
Long-term unemployment arising from mismatches between workers' skills and the demands of a rapidly technological job market.
